blocks.md: This lesson covers the book's section on **Agentic Retrieval**. Read the excerpt, then test yourself below.

blocks.source: Vol III, Long-Term Memory, § Agentic Retrieval
blocks.md: Predicting every file the repair agent will need before invoking the model either stuffs the prompt with irrelevant code or misses a helper dependency that becomes visible only after reading the first stack frame. Forcing the model to search interactively for files the task already named, however, wastes an entire inference turn on a predictable lookup. Two retrieval architectures divide this work differently.

blocks.prompt: Think first: In two or three sentences, explain why Retrieval contract matters for the system this section describes.
blocks.md: Compare your answer with the book's claim: Every read is a bounded request answered by an envelope that reports scope, snapshot, completeness status, and per-item provenance, and an empty result proves nonexistence only for a complete search of the declared scope.

questions.q: The section **Agentic Retrieval** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: Exact lookup, lexical ranking, structural indexes, and dense similarity answer different information needs and fail in different places, and hybrid retrieval joins candidates on full identity.

Every read is a bounded request answered by an envelope that reports scope, snapshot, completeness status, and per-item provenance, and an empty result proves nonexistence only for a complete search of the declared scope.
A session must observe its own committed memory writes on later reads, which a lagging index or replica silently violates unless reads are pinned to a generation at or after the write.

The unit of evaluation is the whole memory policy run through isolated multi-session trials with lifecycle fixtures, scored by task acceptance and cost per accepted task including background maintenance.
